summary:
Marswalk: Know the Way Out, and the Way Back.

On Mars, there is no GPS, rescue team or more than a few hours of spacesuit oxygen. Yet existing Mars maps, such as NASA’s Mars Trek, focus on regional exploration rather than the kilometre-scale decisions astronauts face during an individual excursion.

We developed Marswalk, a browser-based field map for planning and carrying out a single Marswalk (Extravehicular Activity, or EVA) anywhere on Mars. It opens at NASA’s example site, the Mount Sharp boxwork region in Gale Crater, but crews can establish a base and plan routes anywhere on the planet. It supports both pre-mission planning inside a habitat and navigation during an EVA.

Its route-finder ranks paths using a 0–100 safety index, explaining factors including dust, slope, distance, daylight and temperature. A dust-storm layer, built on 13 Martian Years of observations, helps assess seasonal conditions and identify unusual activity.

During an EVA, Marswalk combines optical, thermal, topographic, spectral and atmospheric data from five NASA missions. A live position pointer, oxygen and battery estimates, customisable resource models for different equipment and mission requirements, breadcrumb trail and safety alerts support navigation and decision-making. Offline functionality and large-readout mode make it suitable for field use.

Marswalk helps astronauts and rover teams answer three essential questions: Where am I? What is around me? How do I get home?
details:
Marswalk is a browser-based field mapping and mission-planning tool designed to support astronauts during individual Mars surface excursions, known as Extravehicular Activities (EVAs). Unlike conventional Mars maps that focus on regional or global exploration, Marswalk provides detailed, kilometre-scale information to help crews plan and navigate specific journeys.

It supports two stages of an EVA: pre-mission planning inside a habitat and navigation during the actual excursion. Crews can establish a base anywhere on Mars and plan routes to destinations using an intelligent route-finder. It ranks possible paths using a 0–100 safety index, considering slope, dust activity, distance, daylight and temperature, while explaining the factors behind each score. A dust-storm monitoring layer, based on 13 Martian Years of observations, also helps crews assess seasonal conditions and identify unusual dust activity.

During an EVA, Marswalk integrates optical, thermal, topographic, spectral and atmospheric data from five NASA missions into one interface. A position pointer helps explorers track their location, while an oxygen and battery management system estimates resource consumption and when they should turn back. Its resource models are customisable to accommodate different spacesuit configurations, equipment specifications and mission requirements. Additional features include a breadcrumb trail for retracing routes, safety alerts for changing conditions, offline functionality and a large-readout mode for easier viewing.

Marswalk brings multiple sources of NASA data and essential navigation tools together in one platform, reducing the need to switch between separate maps and datasets. Its route assessment helps crews compare possible paths, while resource estimates support better decisions about how far they can safely travel. Customisable models make it adaptable to different mission profiles rather than restricting users to fixed assumptions. Offline access also makes the platform more suitable for environments with limited connectivity.

Our goal is to make Mars exploration safer and more informed by helping astronauts understand their surroundings, manage limited resources and retrace their journeys. Although designed around human EVAs, Marswalk's mapping and route-planning capabilities could also support robotic rover missions. Ultimately, we hope to contribute to the infrastructure needed for sustained human exploration of Mars.

We developed Marswalk as a browser-based application using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Python. We also utilized Claude to code and debug to speed up our progress and polish our work. These technologies allowed us to create an interactive mapping interface, integrate different datasets and implement features such as route assessment, resource modelling and offline access. We also incorporated data from five NASA missions to provide different views of the Martian surface and environment.

Regarding the heuristic algorithm to measure safety index of a position on the map, we developed a search algorithm with aids of Claude. This is the link to the document about the detail about how the algorithm work : https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/folders/1nRVdA9nduJACcLIg3xP1BLijx5YSjVS4

Our main innovation is treating a Mars map as an operational field tool rather than simply a geographical reference. Instead of only showing astronauts where they are, Marswalk helps them decide where to go, evaluate environmental risks, monitor their resources and find their way back. Combining mission planning, navigation, environmental awareness and adaptable resource modelling into one interface creates a more comprehensive approach to Mars exploration.

We considered the unique challenges of operating on Mars, including the absence of GPS, limited communication, unpredictable environmental conditions, restricted oxygen and battery supplies, and difficult terrain. We also considered the need for accessible information during an EVA, where astronauts may have limited time to interpret complex maps. Consequently, we prioritised clear visualisation, explainable route scores, configurable resource assumptions, offline functionality and large readouts.

We also considered the limitations of our data and models: historical dust observations cannot guarantee future conditions, and estimated resource consumption is not a substitute for certified equipment measurements. Our aim was to create a practical decision-support tool while being transparent about these limitations.
